On the day a report is received, the Administrator stamps it with the receipt date and enters that date and the 10-day due date in the Inspection Log. A copy goes to the governing body the same day.
Within 2 business days of receipt, the Administrator reviews each cited deficiency with the department head or staff member responsible and decides whether to agree with it or dispute it.
If [AGENCY NAME] disagrees with a finding, the Administrator prepares a written statement with supporting evidence. It must reach DCH within 10 days of receipt. Proof of delivery is kept.

For each finding not disputed, the Administrator writes a plan of correction. It states the corrective action, the person responsible, how compliance will be monitored, and a date-certain completion date. The plan must reach DCH within 10 days of receipt.
If DCH provides a website for submitting plans of correction, the Administrator also files the plan electronically within the same 10-day period and keeps the confirmation.
The governing body reviews the plan of correction before or immediately after submission. The governing body's review is recorded in its minutes.

Within 3 business days of submitting the plan, the Administrator posts the most recent inspection report and plan of correction in the [LOCATION, e.g., main lobby] where residents and visitors see information. Posting is limited to the most recent report. Older reports are kept in the inspection file.

If [AGENCY NAME] maintains a website, the Administrator or designee adds or updates a prominent link to all inspection reports and plans of correction from the previous 18 months. The link is checked monthly and the check is logged. Reports older than 18 months may be removed.

The Administrator tracks each corrective action to its due date and gives the governing body a status report at least monthly until all items are complete. The Administrator signs off on completed items and keeps the evidence, such as training sign-in sheets, repair invoices and revised policies.

If DCH issues a notice of sanction, a follow-up visit or another enforcement action, the Administrator notifies the governing body the same day and responds in writing within the time and manner stated in the notice. The Administrator then reviews related policies and training.
Incorporate each inspection's findings into the quality assurance program (GOV-04). Findings that repeat are reported to the governing body for root-cause review.
After each inspection cycle, the Administrator reviews the Inspection Log and this policy, and recommends revisions to the governing body under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Reviews each report and plan of correction, makes sure resources are available to complete corrections, and monitors repeated findings.
Manages the inspection, meets the 10-day deadlines for disputes and plans of correction, posts reports, and tracks corrective actions to completion.

responsibilities.role: On-site manager / senior staff on duty
responsibilities.duty: Greets surveyors, verifies identification, notifies the Administrator, and provides records without delay.
Complete assigned corrective actions by the date-certain stated in the plan and provide evidence of completion.
Maintains the 18-month link to inspection reports and plans of correction.

documentation: Inspection Log (surveyor names, dates, times, records reviewed, report receipt date, due dates)
Inspection reports and exit-conference notes
Written disagreements with supporting evidence and proof of delivery
Plans of correction with date-certain actions, and proof of submission (including electronic confirmation, if applicable)
Corrective action tracking sheets and completion evidence
Governing body minutes reflecting review
Monthly website link checks and posting log

policies.title: Medicaid Waiver (CCSP / SOURCE Alternative Living Services) Participation and HCBS Settings Compliance
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes and Assisted Living Communities that serve, or apply to serve, residents through the Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program (CCSP / SOURCE Alternative Living Services): Administrator, governing body, business office, care staff
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] takes part in Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program as an Alternative Living Services provider. It also ensures that waiver residents live in a setting that meets federal home and community-based services (HCBS) requirements while the community meets all Georgia licensing rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] participates in the Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program (CMS waiver 0112.R08.00) only after Medicaid provider enrollment is complete and only for residents who have been screened and approved through the waiver process. The waiver pays for Alternative Living Services, which are 24-hour personal care supervision in a licensed personal care home. It does not pay room and board, which the resident pays. [AGENCY NAME] treats waiver residents the same as private-pay residents in rights, services and quality of care. The community does not rely on Medicaid revenue in its budget because the waiver is time-limited and is currently scheduled to expire 11/08/2027 unless renewed. Every waiver resident's setting protects privacy, choice, dignity, visitors and freedom from restraint, consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) and Georgia assisted living rules.

definitions.definition: The Community Care Services Program and the Service Options Using Resources in a Community Environment program. Both operate under Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver.
The waiver service that covers 24-hour personal care supervision for eligible residents in a licensed personal care home.
The regional agency, reached through the statewide line 866-552-4464 (866-55-AGING), that performs the first waiver assessment and screening.
Georgia DHS Division of Family and Children Services. It determines Medicaid financial eligibility and keeps the waiting list for the program.
The Georgia Medicaid portal for provider enrollment, revalidation, and provider manuals.
Federal standards that require community settings to protect privacy, resident choice, access to the community, visitors, and freedom from coercion and restraint.
Electronic visit verification, required by the 21st Century Cures Act for certain Medicaid personal care services.

procedures: The Administrator confirms before enrolling that the community holds a current license permitting the services offered, and enrolls through GAMMIS. Enrollment is not retroactive, so no waiver services are billed for any date before enrollment is effective.

The Administrator obtains the current Medicaid Alternative Living Services provider manual and the current per-diem rate from GAMMIS and files both in the Waiver Binder. The Administrator reviews them at enrollment and whenever DCH issues an update.

When a prospective resident or family asks about the waiver, staff explain that assessment is requested from the local AAA at 866-552-4464, that the screening determines eligibility and urgency, and that DFCS decides financial eligibility and keeps the waiting list. Staff do not promise placement, approval or timing.

The Administrator does not hold a bed for a waiver applicant unless the community has first told the applicant in writing the cost of any hold and that waiver payment may not begin until approval and enrollment steps are complete.

Before admission, the Administrator tells the waiver resident and representative in writing that the waiver does not pay room and board. The resident pays the room-and-board rate set by the DHS Division of Aging Services for SOURCE residents (currently reported as $768 per month effective 1/1/2026; the Administrator verifies the current figure before each admission). The resident keeps the rest of the SSI benefit for personal needs. The rate and the personal-needs allowance are written into the admission agreement.

The Administrator applies the same pre-admission screening, assessment and admission criteria (ADM-01, ADM-02) to waiver and private-pay applicants. A person is not admitted if the community cannot meet the resident's needs.

A written care plan is completed within 14 days of admission, updated at least annually and whenever the resident's needs change substantially. It reflects the resident's preferences, goals and chosen activities and is developed with the resident and representative. The plan is coordinated with the waiver case manager's service plan, and a copy is shared with the case manager when authorized.
Periodic or short-term medical and nursing services are not provided as community services. If the resident needs them, staff help the resident and case manager arrange them from an outside provider.

The Administrator reviews the setting each year, and after any physical change, against the HCBS standards. The review checks privacy, choice of activities and schedule, visitors, access to the community, food, telephone access, and freedom from restraint. It is signed and dated and any needed changes are made.

Staff knock and wait for a response before entering a resident's room and allow free, uncensored communication. Residents may have visitors at times that suit them, subject only to a written house rule that does not restrict a right and is applied equally to all residents. House rules and visiting rules are reviewed against HCBS requirements.

The community never locks a resident into or out of the resident's bedroom and never restricts free access to common areas. If a resident or family asks for a resident-controlled bedroom lock, the Administrator consults DCH and the waiver case manager first and approves nothing until DCH confirms in writing that it is allowed. Any approved lock must allow staff emergency access.
Physical and chemical restraints are not used. Staff report any suspected restraint, restriction of rights, or coercion to the Administrator immediately.

The Administrator confirms with DCH, and records the answer in the Waiver Binder, whether electronic visit verification (EVV) applies to the Alternative Living Services placement. For personal support services billed under HCPCS T1019 through CCSP or SOURCE, the Administrator makes sure EVV (Georgia's system, Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+) is set up, staff are trained, and visits are captured before claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026.

The business office bills only for services actually delivered and documented, reconciles each claim to care and attendance records, and follows GOV-05 for billing integrity. The Administrator holds claims that fail EVV or documentation checks until they are corrected.

The Administrator reports quarterly to the governing body on waiver census, waiting applicants, receivables, denials, and the expiration date of the waiver. The annual budget treats Medicaid revenue as uncertain and includes a plan for a change or non-renewal of the waiver.

If DCH, the AAA or the case manager notifies the community of a waiver change, a rate change, a program audit or the end of the waiver, the Administrator informs the governing body within 2 business days and notifies affected residents and representatives in writing, with the appropriate discharge or transfer protections applied under ADM-05.
Discharge or transfer of a waiver resident follows ADM-05 and ADM-06. The Administrator also notifies the case manager.

responsibilities.duty: Approves participation in the waiver, ensures budgets do not depend on Medicaid revenue, and reviews quarterly waiver reports.
Manages enrollment and revalidation, provider manual and rate updates, admission decisions, HCBS setting reviews, EVV readiness, and communication with the AAA, DFCS and case managers.
Verifies rates, bills accurately, reconciles claims, and keeps resident room-and-board accounts.
Deliver personal care and supervision as planned, protect privacy and choice, and complete required EVV and service documentation.
Participates in assessment, care plan updates and coordination with the case manager as authorized.

documentation: GAMMIS enrollment and revalidation confirmations
Waiver Binder: provider manual, rate sheets, DCH notices, EVV confirmation from DCH
Admission agreement with room-and-board and personal-needs terms
Screening/eligibility correspondence (AAA, DFCS, case manager)
Resident assessments and written care plans with updates
Annual HCBS setting review checklist
Claim and EVV reconciliation reports
Quarterly governing body waiver report

policies.title: Resident Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All residents, representatives and legal surrogates; all staff, volunteers and contractors of the Personal Care Home or Assisted Living Community
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident of [AGENCY NAME] is told of, and can exercise, the rights Georgia provides to residents, and to explain the responsibilities that go with them.
policies.policy: Each resident has the rights set out in Rule 111-8-63-.25 and is treated with dignity, respect, choice, independence and privacy. Rights may be waived only by the resident, or by the resident's representative or legal surrogate where the rules allow. The community may not waive rights for the resident. Care is adequate and appropriate. No resident is punished or harassed for enforcing a right. Residents have the right to vote and exercise constitutional rights, choose activities and schedules, interact with the wider community, have privacy in their room with staff knocking first, communicate freely and privately without staff censorship, and be free from coercion to assign money, valuables or property to the community. Married residents may share a room, and no more than two residents share a bedroom. A resident who has no court commitment and no authorized representative may self-discharge on 30 days' written notice. No member of the governing body, administration or staff, or their family members, may serve as a resident's legal surrogate (Rule 111-8-62-.03).

definitions.definition: A person the resident has authorized, or who is legally authorized, to act for the resident, such as an agent under a power of attorney, within the limits of that authority.
A person authorized by law or court to make decisions for a resident. No governing body member, administrator, staff member or their family member may serve in this role.
A voluntary, informed decision by the resident, or an authorized representative or legal surrogate as allowed by rule, to give up a specific right.
The written statement of resident rights that each resident or representative signs at admission and that is kept in the resident file.

procedures: At or before admission, the Administrator or designee gives each resident and representative a copy of the Resident's Rights form and the community's house rules. Staff review them aloud in plain language and answer questions. Interpretation or other accommodations are provided under RR-08.
The resident or representative signs and dates the Resident's Rights form. A signed copy is placed in the resident file (Rule 111-8-63-.24), and a copy is given to the resident.
The Administrator posts a summary of resident rights in a common area, along with the assigned ombudsman's name, address and telephone number (RR-03).

All staff are trained on resident rights within 60 days of hire and as part of each year's continuing education. Training covers every right listed in this policy, and attendance is recorded in the training record.

Staff knock and wait for permission before entering a resident's bedroom, except in an emergency. Staff protect privacy during personal care by closing doors and curtains and exposing only what is necessary.

Staff support residents who want to vote, practice their religion, take part in community activities, or choose their own schedules, including when to wake, sleep, eat and go out. The Administrator helps arrange voter registration, absentee ballots or transport where requested.

Residents may send and receive mail unopened, use a private telephone, and speak privately with visitors, the ombudsman, government officials and their own advisers. Staff do not read, censor or hold back communications.
The community does not lock a resident into or out of the bedroom and does not restrict free access to common areas.
Married residents who wish to share a room are accommodated when space is available. No more than two residents may share a bedroom. Roommate pairings are by choice and compatibility where possible.

No employee or the community may ask or pressure a resident to give or assign money, valuables or property. Staff report any such request or offer to the Administrator the same day, and the Administrator reviews it under RR-05 and GOV-05.

If a resident or representative wants to waive a right, the Administrator explains the right and its effect and documents the request in writing, with the resident's or representative's signature, in the resident file. The Administrator does not accept a waiver of rights in advance as a condition of admission.

The Administrator checks that no governing body member, administrator, staff member or relative of one is named as a resident's legal surrogate. A copy of every power of attorney is kept in the resident file. If a conflict is found, the Administrator informs the resident and representative in writing and takes appropriate steps.

If a resident wants to self-discharge, staff tell the Administrator, who confirms there is no court commitment or authorized representative and that the resident has the capacity to give notice. The resident gives 30 days' written notice, and the Administrator coordinates a safe transition under ADM-05.

Staff report any suspected violation of rights, retaliation, abuse, neglect or exploitation to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates under RR-02 and reports to the appropriate agency as required. Retaliation or harassment of any resident or staff member who asserts a right results in discipline up to termination.
The Administrator reviews rights practices at least annually, using resident feedback, complaint logs and observations, and reports to the governing body.

Residents are asked to respect other residents' rights and property, follow house rules that do not restrict a right, pay fees under the admission agreement, tell staff about changes in their health, and give notice of absence or departure. A resident's failure to meet a responsibility does not remove a right.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts policies that support dignity, choice, independence and privacy, and reviews reports on rights compliance.
Distributes and explains rights at admission, posts rights information, trains staff, reviews waivers and surrogate conflicts, and investigates alleged violations.
Respect each right in daily care, knock before entering, and report suspected violations.
Sign the rights form, ask questions, and follow the community's lawful house rules and the terms of the admission agreement.

documentation: Signed Resident's Rights form in each resident file
Written waivers of rights, if any
Copies of powers of attorney and surrogate documents in the resident file
Staff training records on resident rights
Self-discharge notices
Investigation records of alleged rights violations
Annual rights practices review

policies.title: Grievances, Complaints and Resident Feedback
policies.applies_to: Residents, representatives, family members, staff; Administrator and on-site managers
policies.purpose: To give residents and representatives a clear, safe way to raise complaints and offer feedback, and to make sure each one is investigated and answered and used to improve the community.
policies.policy: Residents and representatives may complain or give feedback to [AGENCY NAME] at any time, orally or in writing, without fear of retaliation. The admission agreement describes how the community responds to formal complaints and how a resident or representative files one (Rule 111-8-63-.16). No resident is punished or harassed for enforcing rights (Rule 111-8-63-.25). Residents are also told that they may contact the assigned long-term care ombudsman and the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH) Healthcare Facility Regulation Division directly. The community never discourages or prevents a complaint to an outside agency. All complaints are logged, investigated, answered and reviewed in the quality assurance program.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction about care, services, staff, other residents, the physical setting, charges or rights, whether or not the person calls it a complaint.
A complaint made in writing, or an oral complaint that the person asks to be handled formally, which the community logs and answers in writing.
Any adverse action, such as threats, reduced care, a change of room, or pressure to leave, taken because someone complained or asserted a right.

procedures: The admission agreement and a posted notice in the [LOCATION] explain how to file a complaint, who receives it, and that the person may use the Administrator, the on-site manager, the ombudsman or DCH. Staff review the process with each resident and representative at admission.

Complaint forms and a locked or private drop box are kept in [LOCATION]. A resident or representative may also complain by phone to [PHONE] or in person to any staff member. Staff help residents who need assistance to write or submit a complaint.

Any staff member who receives a complaint records it the same shift on the Complaint Log form, noting the date, time, complainant, summary and the staff member's name, and gives it to the Administrator or on-site manager by the next business day.
The Administrator or designee acknowledges the complaint to the complainant within 2 business days, in the way the complainant prefers.

If a complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, a rights violation or an immediate risk to health or safety, the Administrator acts at once to protect the resident, separates the persons involved if necessary, and starts the incident reporting and investigation process in the community's abuse and incident policies. Required reports to DCH, adult protective services or law enforcement are made without delay.

For other complaints, the Administrator or designee investigates promptly by interviewing the complainant and relevant staff and residents, reviewing records, and examining the setting. The person investigating must not have been directly involved in the complaint.

The Administrator sends a written response to the complainant, normally within 10 business days of receipt. It states what was found, what action was taken or planned, and whom to contact if the person is not satisfied. If more time is needed, the Administrator explains in writing and gives a date.

If the complainant is not satisfied, the Administrator offers a meeting with the Administrator and, if the complainant wishes, the governing body representative [NAME/TITLE]. The complainant may bring a family member, representative or ombudsman.

Residents and representatives are given the assigned ombudsman's name, address and phone number, posted in a common area (RR-03), and are told they may also complain to DCH HFRD (pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov). Staff do not discourage or impede any complaint to an outside agency and are trained to provide the contact information on request.

Staff do not retaliate against any resident or representative who complains. Any suspected retaliation is reported to the Administrator and investigated. Substantiated retaliation results in discipline up to termination.
Staff must not ask a resident to withdraw a complaint or to sign a statement that no problem exists.

The Administrator offers residents regular opportunities for feedback. The community holds resident meetings at least quarterly to hear suggestions on meals, activities, services and house rules, and gives each resident or representative a satisfaction survey at least annually. Records of meetings and survey results are kept and the community's responses are shared with residents.

The Administrator reviews the Complaint Log monthly for trends, such as repeated complaints about a person, unit, shift or service, and reports results to the quality assurance committee (GOV-04) and to the governing body at least quarterly.
Complaints received through DCH or the ombudsman are logged, investigated and answered in the same way, and any required response to DCH is made within the deadlines in GOV-07.

Complaint files are kept for at least [RETENTION PERIOD] and are available to DCH inspectors. Complaint information is kept confidential and shared only with those who need it to resolve the matter (RR-07).

responsibilities.duty: Receives, investigates and answers complaints, protects residents during investigations, prevents retaliation, runs resident meetings and surveys, and reports trends.
Accept any complaint, record it the same shift, assist residents who need help to complain, and never discourage a complaint.
Hears unresolved complaints and reviews trend reports.
May file a complaint in any form, and is asked to give enough information to allow an investigation.

documentation: Complaint Log and complaint forms
Investigation notes and evidence
Written responses to complainants
Resident meeting minutes and survey results
Quarterly trend reports to QA committee and governing body
Admission agreement complaint-process provision
Posted ombudsman and DCH contact notice

policies.title: Ombudsman Access
policies.applies_to: All residents and representatives; all staff, volunteers, contractors and visitors
policies.purpose: To protect each resident's right to contact and meet with the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program and to make sure the ombudsman is always visible and reachable.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to access the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program (O.C.G.A. 31-8-50 et seq.; Rule 111-8-63-.25). [AGENCY NAME] posts the name, address and telephone number of the ombudsman assigned to the community in a common area, and does not impede ombudsman visits, communications or private conversations with residents. The community does not retaliate against any resident or staff member for contacting the ombudsman.

definitions.definition: The state program, operating under the federal Older Americans Act, that advocates for residents of long-term care facilities, including personal care homes and assisted living communities, and resolves complaints on their behalf.
The regional ombudsman or representative designated to serve the community's area.
The regional aging agency reached statewide at 866-552-4464 (866-55-AGING).

procedures: Within 30 days of licensure or opening, the Administrator contacts the AAA at 866-552-4464 to confirm the name of the ombudsman assigned to the community and the ombudsman's direct address and telephone number.

The Administrator posts a notice in [COMMON AREA LOCATION] stating the ombudsman's name ([OMBUDSMAN NAME]), address ([OMBUDSMAN ADDRESS]) and phone ([OMBUDSMAN PHONE]), in at least 14-point type at a height that a seated resident can read. The notice stays posted at all times.

The Administrator checks the posting at least monthly and replaces it within 5 business days of learning of any change in the assigned ombudsman or contact details. Each check is recorded in the Posting Log.
At admission, staff tell every resident and representative about the ombudsman's role, give them the contact information in writing, and note this in the admission checklist.
The admission agreement and the complaint process (RR-02) refer residents to the ombudsman as an independent option.

Staff allow the ombudsman access to the community during visits, and let the ombudsman talk with any resident privately, in a room or area chosen by the resident, without staff present, unless the resident asks otherwise.

If an ombudsman arrives, the first staff member on duty greets the ombudsman, asks for identification, and notifies the Administrator or manager. The Administrator provides requested information consistent with RR-07 and the law, including resident records for which the resident has given consent or as otherwise authorized by law.

Staff do not screen, delay, listen in on, or discourage resident calls, letters, visits or meetings with the ombudsman, and do not require advance notice from a resident wanting to speak with the ombudsman.
A resident who wishes to contact the ombudsman may use the private telephone (Rule 111-8-63-.17) and staff provide help dialing, writing or mailing if asked.
The Administrator invites the ombudsman to speak at resident meetings or participate in resident events where the ombudsman wishes.
The Administrator investigates and responds to ombudsman referrals and complaints in the same way as other complaints under RR-02 and cooperates in resolution.

Staff are trained on this policy within 60 days of hire and annually. Any suspected interference with ombudsman access or retaliation is reported to the Administrator and results in discipline up to termination.
The Administrator records each ombudsman visit and referral and reports a summary to the quality assurance committee quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms and posts the assigned ombudsman's information, keeps it current, ensures access, and responds to ombudsman referrals.
Provide contact information on request, facilitate private contact, and never impede or discourage ombudsman access.
May contact the ombudsman at any time, and may decide whether to meet privately.

documentation: Posted ombudsman notice and monthly Posting Log
Admission checklist showing ombudsman information provided
Ombudsman visit and referral log
Staff training records
Complaint records for ombudsman referrals

policies.title: Admission Agreement, Fees, Rate Increases, Deposits and Refunds
policies.applies_to: Administrator, business office, admissions staff; all applicants, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident or representative receives a clear written agreement that states all fees, that charge increases are noticed in advance, and that refunds are handled fairly and promptly.
policies.policy: Every resident, or the representative, signs a written admission agreement before or at admission. It is written in plain, understandable language and is consistent with the community's licensed residential care profile (Rule 111-8-63-.16). The agreement lists all fees and charges, whether daily, weekly or monthly, and says what each covers, including any service charged for separately. [AGENCY NAME] gives written notice at least 30 days before any increase in personal-service charges and at least 60 days before any increase in room-and-board charges. The agreement contains a refund policy covering death, transfer and discharge. The agreement may not waive any resident right (Rule 111-8-63-.25), and no resident is coerced to assign money, valuables or property to the community.

definitions.definition: The written contract between the community and the resident or representative setting out services, charges, rights and responsibilities.
Charges for care and services provided to the resident, such as assistance with activities of daily living and other personal services.
Charges for the resident's room, meals and related housing costs.
The community's profile on file with DCH describing the services, populations served and limits of care the community is authorized to provide.
Money paid before or at admission to hold or reserve a room or to secure charges, which is refundable as stated in the agreement.

procedures: The Administrator maintains one standard admission agreement, reviewed by the governing body and by legal counsel, and compares it each time the licensed residential care profile is updated to confirm that the services, fees and limits of care are consistent with the profile (GOV-06).

The agreement is written in plain language at about a [READING LEVEL] reading level and is available in other languages or formats on request (RR-08). Staff do not use legal or technical terms without explaining them.

Before the agreement is signed, the Administrator or designee gives the applicant and representative a copy and reviews it in person at least [NUMBER] days before the planned admission date where possible, and allows time to read it and take it to an advisor.

The agreement states every fee and charge, whether daily, weekly or monthly, what each covers, and which services are optional and cost extra. It states how and when payment is due and how charges are billed.

The agreement describes the continuous assessment of the resident and the circumstances in which the community will refer or transfer the resident because of a change in condition, consistent with ADM-02, ADM-04 and ADM-05.

The agreement describes the complaint process (RR-02) and transportation provisions, including that emergency transportation is available at all times and who bears the cost of non-emergency transport.

The agreement includes the refund policy for death, transfer and discharge, including how unused prepaid amounts and deposits are calculated, which charges (if any) are retained, and the deadline for returning money, which is [REFUND DEADLINE IN DAYS] days. The refund policy applies equally to all residents.

The agreement states the written discharge and transfer procedure and 30-day notice (ADM-05), and the resident's right to self-discharge on 30 days' written notice if no court commitment or authorized representative applies (RR-01).
The agreement describes the Resident's Rights form and house rules, and does not ask a resident to waive any right or release the community from liability for its own negligence.
The resident or representative, and the Administrator, sign and date the agreement. The resident or representative receives a copy at signing, and the original is kept in the resident file (RR-07).

Before raising personal-service charges, the Administrator prepares a written notice stating the old and new charge, the effective date and the reason, and delivers it to the resident and representative at least 30 days before the effective date. Before raising room-and-board charges, the notice is delivered at least 60 days before the effective date. Delivery is by hand with a signed receipt or by mail with proof of mailing.

A rate increase takes effect no earlier than the notice period allows. If the notice is late, the increase is delayed until the full notice period has passed. A change to a resident's charges because of a care plan change the resident agreed to is documented in the care plan and a written amendment to the agreement.

The business office issues an itemized statement each billing period. Deposits are held in [ACCOUNT TYPE] and recorded in the resident's account. The community does not require a deposit that is not described in the agreement.

When a resident dies, transfers or is discharged, the business office calculates the refund within 5 business days using the agreement's refund policy, prepares an itemized final statement, and sends the refund and statement to the resident or the estate or representative by the deadline in the agreement. Personal property and funds are returned under RR-05.

If a resident is receiving Medicaid waiver services, the agreement explains that the waiver does not pay room and board, states the room-and-board amount the resident pays, and the resident's personal-needs allowance (GOV-08).

The Administrator reviews the agreement at least annually and whenever rules, the licensed residential care profile or fees change. Residents with existing agreements receive a written amendment for any changes, with the required notice. Questions about the agreement or billing are handled under RR-02.
Refund requests, disputes and notices are recorded in the business office file, and refund timeliness is reported to the quality assurance committee quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the admission agreement form, fee schedule and refund policy, and any rate increases.
Ensures the agreement meets rule requirements and matches the licensed residential care profile, reviews it with applicants, issues rate-increase notices and approves refunds.
Prepares itemized statements, handles deposits, calculates and issues refunds on time, and keeps proof of notices.
Reads the agreement, asks questions, signs, pays charges when due, and gives notice as required.

documentation: Signed admission agreement in the resident file
Current fee schedule and agreement template with revision dates
Rate-increase notices with proof of delivery and effective dates
Itemized billing statements and deposit receipts
Refund calculations, itemized final statements and proof of refund
Written amendments to the agreement
Annual agreement review record

policies.title: Resident Funds and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: PCH (2–24 beds) and ALC (25+ beds): administrator, on-site manager, business office staff, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To protect each resident's money, valuables and personal property, to keep accurate records that can be inspected by the resident, the representative and DCH, and to make sure no resident is pressured to hand over money or property to the community or its staff.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects each resident's right to control his or her own money and belongings. The community will not coerce or pressure any resident to assign money, valuables, benefits or property to the community other than as payment for services under the admission agreement (63-.25). Where a resident asks the community to hold money or valuables for safekeeping, or to make purchases for the resident, the community will keep a written record of every transaction, with an itemized receipt for each deposit and disbursement (63-.24). Valuables held in safekeeping are receipted at admission and each time the resident entrusts more property. An inventory of the resident's valuable personal items is kept in the resident file and updated at any time on the resident's request. Copies of any power of attorney, or any court or Social Security Administration document designating a financial manager, are kept in the resident file. No member of the governing body, administration or staff, and no family member of any of them, may serve as a resident's legal surrogate (62-.03). Residents on the Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP or SOURCE) pay the published room-and-board amount and keep the rest of their income for personal needs; the community will not require any further payment from waiver income.

definitions.definition: Money or valuables a resident voluntarily asks the community to hold in a secure location on the resident's behalf, documented by a signed receipt.
A person legally authorized to act for a resident. Governing body members, administrators, staff and their family members may not serve in this role.
The person the resident has designated, or who is legally authorized, to act for or assist the resident, as defined in Chapter 111-8-62 and Chapter 111-8-63.

The portion of a waiver resident's income remaining after the monthly room-and-board payment. In 2026 the published figures are $768 room and board and $226 left from a $994 SSI benefit; the community will confirm the current amount with DHS Division of Aging Services each January.
A written record showing date, amount, purpose, payee or source and the signature of the staff member and, where possible, the resident or representative.

procedures: At pre-admission and again at admission, the administrator or on-site manager explains to the resident and representative that the resident may manage his or her own money and property, and that the community will hold funds or valuables only if the resident or representative asks in writing.

The community will not require any resident to sign over money, benefits, property or valuables as a condition of admission or continued residence, other than the payments stated in the admission agreement. Any staff member who is asked or pressured by anyone to take such an assignment reports it to the administrator immediately.

At admission, the on-site manager and the resident (or representative) complete a written inventory of valuable personal items the resident brings. Both sign and date it, the resident receives a copy, and the original is placed in the resident file.

The inventory is updated whenever the resident asks, whenever a valuable item is added or removed, and at each care plan review. Each update is dated and initialed by the staff member and the resident or representative.

If a resident asks the community to hold money or valuables, the on-site manager completes a safekeeping form, issues a signed receipt at that time, and gives a copy to the resident or representative. A new receipt is issued each time the resident entrusts additional property.

Funds held for residents are kept in a locked location (or a separate account where an amount is held for the resident), apart from the community's operating funds. Only the administrator, on-site manager and one designated business office employee have access.
For every deposit or disbursement of resident money, staff complete a transaction entry on the resident's ledger the same day and attach an itemized receipt. Two staff members verify any cash count.

A resident or representative may withdraw funds or retrieve valuables on request during normal business hours and, for urgent needs, by arrangement with the on-site manager. The withdrawal is recorded and signed for.

The business office reconciles each resident ledger to the cash or account balance monthly. The administrator reviews and signs the reconciliation. Any discrepancy is investigated within 24 hours and reported to the resident or representative.

Each month the community gives the resident or representative a written statement of activity for funds held. Waiver residents' personal-needs funds are tracked separately from room-and-board payments.

The on-site manager obtains a copy of every power of attorney and any court or SSA document designating a financial manager, and places it in the resident file at admission or when it is first presented.

Before accepting any person as a resident's surrogate or financial contact, the administrator confirms that the person is not a member of the governing body, administration or staff, or a family member of one. If a conflict exists, the administrator informs the resident and representative that the person cannot serve in that role.

Staff may not borrow from, accept gifts or loans from, hold a power of attorney for, serve as a named beneficiary for, or sell anything to a resident. Violations are reported to the administrator and handled under the corporate compliance and personnel policies.

If property or money is reported missing, the staff member who receives the report notifies the on-site manager immediately. The administrator begins an investigation promptly, informs the resident and representative, documents findings, and reports to law enforcement or other authorities if abuse, exploitation or theft is suspected.

At discharge, transfer or death, the on-site manager returns held funds, valuables and inventoried items to the resident or authorized person against a signed receipt and a final accounting, reconciling to the inventory and the safekeeping record.
Each resident's ledger, receipts, inventory and safekeeping record are filed in the resident file and are open to the resident, the representative and DCH for inspection and copying.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure no coercion occurs, approve procedures, review monthly reconciliations, investigate discrepancies and loss reports, and screen proposed surrogates for conflicts.
Complete inventories and safekeeping receipts, supervise transactions and file all records in the resident file.
Maintain ledgers and receipts, reconcile accounts monthly, and keep resident funds separate from operating funds.
Never accept money, gifts or property from residents; document and report loss or pressure concerns immediately.
Decide whether to entrust money or valuables, and review and sign receipts and statements.

documentation: Record of monetary transactions with itemized receipts for every disbursement and deposit
Safekeeping record and signed receipts for monies and valuables held
Resident inventory of valuable personal items with update history
Copies of powers of attorney and court or SSA financial-manager documents
Monthly reconciliation signed by the administrator
Loss or theft reports and investigation notes

policies.title: Advance Directives, DNR Orders and End-of-Life Wishes
policies.applies_to: PCH (2–24 beds) and ALC (25+ beds): administrator, on-site manager, all direct care staff, nursing staff
policies.purpose: To respect each resident's decisions about end-of-life care, to make sure advance directives and DNR orders are in the resident file and known to staff, and to define exactly what staff do when a resident is found unresponsive.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] makes Georgia advance directive forms available to every resident at admission and at any later time on request. Copies of any living will or durable power of attorney for health care executed before 2007, or an executed Georgia advance directive for health care, and any signed medical orders affecting end-of-life care (such as a DNR order), are kept in the resident file (63-.24). Staff follow the unresponsive-resident protocol in 63-.26 without exception: a hospice plan comes first, then the health care agent, then a valid DNR honored in good faith, and otherwise EMS and CPR unless the resident's condition is clearly futile and no physician, authorized RN or physician assistant is on site. The community does not require a resident to have or to waive an advance directive as a condition of admission. All direct care staff are trained in CPR with return demonstration within 60 days of hire.

definitions.definition: A Georgia advance directive for health care, or a living will or durable power of attorney for health care (DPOA-HC) executed before 2007, stating the resident's treatment wishes or naming a health care agent.
The person named by the resident under O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq. to make health care decisions when the resident cannot.
A signed medical order directing that CPR not be started if the resident has no pulse or is not breathing.
A resident who cannot be roused and who shows no signs of normal response, including a resident who may be without pulse or breathing.
A registered nurse or physician assistant authorized under Georgia law to make a determination about a resident's condition.
A resident receiving services from a licensed hospice, with a hospice plan of care on file.

procedures: At admission the on-site manager gives the resident and representative blank Georgia advance directive forms, explains that they are optional, and offers to help the resident get them reviewed by an attorney, physician or other advisor of the resident's choice.
The on-site manager asks whether the resident has a living will, DPOA-HC, advance directive, DNR order or hospice plan, and records the answer in the admission checklist.

Any document provided is copied and placed in the resident file the same day. Originals are returned to the resident or representative, or held in safekeeping only on written request and with a receipt.

Signed medical orders affecting end-of-life care are obtained from the resident's physician and filed. A copy is placed in a clearly marked, immediately accessible location (such as the front of the file or the emergency information sheet) so that any staff member on duty can find it in seconds.

The emergency information sheet for each resident lists code status, the name and phone number of the health care agent, hospice name and phone number if enrolled, physician, and preferred hospital. It is updated within 24 hours of any change.
The care plan states the resident's end-of-life wishes. The plan is reviewed with the resident or representative at admission, at each care plan update, and after any significant change in condition.

If a resident is found unresponsive, the first staff member on the scene calls for help, checks for breathing and pulse, and immediately checks the emergency information sheet while a second staff member brings it.
If the resident is a hospice enrollee: call the hospice first; then call the health care agent; then, if no DNR order exists, call 911 and start CPR.

If the resident has a valid DNR order: honor it in good faith, do not start CPR, notify the hospice (if enrolled), the physician, the health care agent and the representative or legal surrogate, and call the administrator.
If the resident has a health care agent and no DNR: call the agent. If the agent cannot be reached and there is no DNR order, call 911 and start CPR.
If there is no hospice, DNR order or advance directive: call 911 and start CPR, unless the resident's condition is clearly futile and no physician, authorized RN or PA is on site.

Staff must have ready access to emergency numbers and resident information at all times, including during transport. A staff member sends the emergency information sheet and medication list with the resident to the hospital.

Staff notify the representative or legal surrogate and the administrator as soon as the emergency response is under way, and record the change in condition, actions taken and times in the resident file.

The administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause of any accident, injury or death, reports to the representative or legal surrogate, and keeps copies in the resident file and in the central quality assurance file.
If staff are uncertain whether a document is valid or applicable, they act under the next level of the protocol, call 911, and ask the administrator and physician to resolve the question afterward.

The administrator verifies every direct care staff member completes CPR training with return demonstration within 60 days of hire and keeps the roster and certificates in the training records. Staff review this policy at orientation and annually.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure the protocol is followed, staff are trained, investigations start immediately and QA review occurs.
Offer forms, file directives and DNR orders, keep emergency information sheets current.
Assist with resident education, verify orders, and advise staff on clinical questions.
Know where to find code status, follow the unresponsive-resident protocol, and document the response.

responsibilities.role: Resident, representative or health care agent
responsibilities.duty: Provide current documents and notify the community of changes in wishes.

documentation: Copies of living will, DPOA-HC or Georgia advance directive in the resident file
Signed medical orders affecting end-of-life care (for example DNR)
Emergency information sheet for each resident
Care plan entry on end-of-life wishes
Incident and change-in-condition notes, including notifications and times
Investigation reports in the resident file and central QA file
CPR training records with return demonstration

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: PCH (2–24 beds) and ALC (25+ beds): all staff, volunteers and contractors with access to resident or personnel information
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of resident and staff information, to limit disclosure to those permitted by law, and to make sure residents and representatives can inspect and copy their own records.
policies.policy: Personal information in each resident file is confidential. [AGENCY NAME] discloses it only to the resident, the representative or legal surrogate, authorized agents of DCH, and anyone with the written authorization of the resident, representative or legal surrogate (63-.24). The file is available for inspection and copying by the resident, representative or surrogate and by DCH on request. Personnel files are kept confidential but are open to DCH (63-.09), and staff health information is retained in a form that can be retrieved for DCH. Reports of incidents filed with DCH are filed in confidence. Residents have the right to private communication and to privacy in their rooms, and staff knock before entering (63-.25). The community will determine whether it is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, because it conducts standard electronic transactions such as billing Medicaid for waiver services); if so, it will comply with 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164.

definitions.definition: The individual file kept by the administrator or on-site manager for each resident, containing identifying, health, financial and legal information.
A signed, dated release from the resident, representative or legal surrogate naming the person or organization allowed to receive specified information.
A health plan, clearinghouse, or health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard transactions covered by HIPAA.
Individually identifiable health information, in any form, held by a covered entity.
The notice a covered entity must give to individuals describing how health information is used and disclosed and their rights (45 CFR 164.520).

procedures: Within 30 days of the permit being issued and before accepting any billing for Medicaid waiver services, the administrator reviews with counsel or a compliance consultant whether the community is a HIPAA covered entity and documents the determination in the compliance file. The determination is reviewed whenever billing practices change.

If the community is a covered entity, the administrator designates a privacy official and a contact person for complaints, adopts HIPAA privacy and security procedures, and conducts a security risk analysis under 45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C.

If the community is a covered entity, a Notice of Privacy Practices is given to each resident at admission, a good-faith acknowledgement is requested and documented, and the notice is posted and available on request (164.520).
If the community is a covered entity, workforce members receive privacy training at hire and when procedures change, and sanctions for violations are applied and documented (164.530).
All staff, volunteers and contractors sign a confidentiality agreement at hire. Orientation covers what information is confidential and the consequences of misuse.

Resident files are kept in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system. Only the administrator, on-site manager, nursing staff and those with a job need may access a file. Files are not left open in common areas.

Medication administration records, care plans and emergency information sheets are kept where staff who need them can reach them but visitors cannot view them. Whiteboards and sign-in sheets do not display diagnoses or other health information.

Staff do not discuss residents' health or personal matters in hallways, dining areas or public places, or with other residents or visitors. Staff do not post resident information or photographs on social media.

Before disclosing any information, the staff member confirms that the requester is the resident, the representative or legal surrogate, a DCH agent with identification, or a person holding a current written authorization in the file. If unsure, the staff member refers the request to the administrator.

Written authorizations are specific as to person, information, purpose and expiration and may be revoked in writing. The on-site manager files each authorization and each revocation in the resident file.

Required disclosures and care-related disclosures (for example to the resident's physician, hospital or pharmacy during treatment, transfer or emergency, or to agencies in an abuse investigation) are made only to the extent permitted by law. The staff member records what was disclosed, to whom and when.

When a resident or representative asks to inspect or copy the file, the on-site manager arranges access promptly during business hours, supervises the inspection and provides copies. Copy requests are logged. A DCH inspector is given immediate access on request.

Staff health information, including TB screening and physical examination results, is retained in a retrievable format and kept separate from resident records. Personnel files are confidential, locked, and available to DCH.
Any report of an incident filed with DCH is sent in confidence, copies are kept in the central QA file, and are shared inside the community only with those who need them.
Residents' mail, telephone calls and visits are private. Staff do not open resident mail or listen to calls, and each resident has private telephone access.
Staff knock and wait for a response before entering a resident's room, except in an emergency. Personal care is provided with door and curtains closed.

A staff member who learns of an unauthorized use or disclosure of resident information reports it to the administrator immediately. The administrator investigates, mitigates harm, notifies the affected resident or representative, and, if the community is a covered entity, evaluates breach notification duties under 45 CFR Part 164. Corrective action is documented.

Records are retained and destroyed only according to the community's retention schedule and in a manner that protects confidentiality (shredding or secure electronic deletion). Personnel files are kept for 3 years after the employee leaves.

responsibilities.duty: Make and document the HIPAA status determination, enforce confidentiality, investigate breaches, and give DCH access.
Maintain HIPAA procedures, notices, training and complaint handling.
Control access to resident files, process authorizations and requests for inspection or copies.
Keep information confidential, disclose only as permitted and report suspected violations.
Sign authorizations as desired and may inspect and copy the file.

documentation: HIPAA covered-entity determination and, if applicable, HIPAA policies, risk analysis and training records
Signed staff confidentiality agreements
Written authorizations and revocations in resident files
Log of file inspections, copy requests and DCH access
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgements (if covered entity)
Records of unauthorized disclosures and corrective action
Retention and destruction log

policies.title: Nondiscrimination, Disability Access and Language Access
policies.applies_to: PCH (2–24 beds) and ALC (25+ beds): administrator, admissions staff, all staff
federal: ADA Title III, 42 U.S.C. 12181 et seq.
Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. 3601 et seq.
policies.purpose: To ensure that applicants and residents are treated without discrimination, that people with disabilities and people with limited English proficiency have equal access to services, and that decisions about admission rest on the objective criteria in the rule.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, religion, disability, age, familial status or any other characteristic protected by federal or Georgia law. Admission decisions follow the objective criteria in 63-.15(1): age 18 or older, no active TB, no need for continuous medical or nursing care, no need for restraint or confinement for behavioral control, ability to participate in transfers, and ability to take part in social and leisure activities. The community provides reasonable accommodations and communication aids for residents with disabilities, and takes reasonable steps to give meaningful access to residents with limited English proficiency, including interpreters and translated key documents. No resident will be punished or harassed for enforcing his or her rights (63-.25). The English-proficiency requirement for staff assisting with self-administered medications (63-.20) is a safety qualification for that task only and is not a basis for denying service to residents who speak other languages.

definitions.definition: A change in rules, policies, practices or services, or a physical modification, that gives a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the community, unless it would cause undue hardship or fundamentally alter the service.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English such that a person needs language help to communicate effectively.
Services or devices that give effective communication to people with hearing, vision or speech disabilities, such as qualified interpreters, large print, captioning or assistive listening.
The written criteria, based on 63-.15(1), applied equally to all applicants.
Punishment, harassment or adverse treatment of a person for asserting rights or filing a complaint.

procedures: The administrator designates a nondiscrimination and accessibility coordinator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME] unless another person is named in writing) and posts the coordinator's name and phone number [PHONE] in a common area.

Admissions staff apply the written objective criteria in 63-.15(1) to every applicant and document the basis for each admission or denial in the pre-admission file. A denial reason must relate to a listed criterion or to the community's documented inability to meet the person's needs, never to a protected characteristic.

Admissions staff do not ask about or consider race, religion, national origin, familial status or similar characteristics in deciding admission. The same admission agreement, rates and house rules apply to all residents in the same service category.

A resident's disability, diagnosis or need for assistance is not itself a reason for denial. Admissions staff evaluate whether the community can meet the person's needs with reasonable accommodations and with the services the community is permitted to provide.

Applicants and residents may request an accommodation orally or in writing at any time. The coordinator documents the request, discusses options with the person, responds within 5 business days (sooner if urgent), and records the decision and reasons. A denial is reviewed by the administrator.

Common accommodations include grab bars or room modifications at the resident's request, allowing assistive animals, alternate dining or activity arrangements, large-print or read-aloud materials, and accessible routes. The administrator confirms with the resident what works and updates the care plan.

For residents who are deaf or hard of hearing, blind or low vision, or who have speech or cognitive disabilities, staff use effective communication methods, such as written notes, large print, qualified interpreters or assistive devices, at no charge to the resident.
At pre-admission, staff ask each applicant and representative the preferred language for communication and for written materials, and record it in the resident file and care plan.

For residents with limited English proficiency, the community arranges a qualified interpreter (in person, by phone or video) for the assessment, admission agreement, rights review, care planning and consent discussions, and for grievances and medical decisions. Family members or other residents are used only if the resident requests it and the administrator agrees.

The administrator identifies the languages most commonly spoken by residents and applicants in the area, and arranges translated versions of the Resident's Rights form, the grievance procedure, the admission agreement summary and key notices, or provides oral interpretation of them with documentation.
A notice, posted in common areas and given at admission, informs residents of the right to language assistance and accommodations and of the grievance process, in the languages identified.

Staff who assist with self-administered medications must be proficient in English and able to read, write and follow written instructions in English, as 63-.20 requires. The administrator schedules and assigns tasks so that residents who speak other languages still have interpretive support when medications are given.

Direct care staff receive training at orientation and annually on nondiscrimination, dignity and respect, effective communication with people with disabilities, working with interpreters, and the prohibition on retaliation.

Residents may file a complaint of discrimination or denied accommodation under RR-02 (Grievances) or with the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman, DCH or federal civil rights agencies. Staff direct anyone who raises such a concern to the coordinator and provide the grievance form. No resident will be punished or harassed for enforcing his or her rights.

The coordinator investigates discrimination complaints promptly, documents findings and corrective action, and reports each complaint and outcome to the administrator and to the QA committee quarterly.

The administrator reviews physical accessibility of the building and the website and marketing materials at least annually and when plans change, and documents barriers identified and correction plans.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure nondiscriminatory admission, review denials, approve accommodations and arrange interpreters and translations.
Receive and track accommodation requests and complaints and report to QA.
Apply objective criteria, document the basis for decisions and ask about language needs.
Treat all residents with dignity, use interpreters and aids, and report concerns.

documentation: Pre-admission evaluations showing the objective criteria applied and the basis for each decision
Accommodation request log and decisions
Language preference record in each resident file
Interpreter use log and translated-document list
Nondiscrimination and language-access training records
Complaint and investigation records
Annual accessibility review

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: PCH (2–24 beds) and ALC (25+ beds): administrator, on-site manager, admissions staff, nursing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that only people the community is permitted and able to serve are admitted, that each applicant is evaluated and the evaluation is documented, and that admission safety measures, including checks for sex offenders and violent offenders, are met.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits only adults age 18 or older who do not have active TB; who do not need continuous medical or nursing care and treatment; who do not need physical or chemical restraints, isolation or confinement for behavioral control; who can actively participate in transfers; and who can take part in the community's social and leisure activities (63-.15). The administrator or on-site manager evaluates and documents whether the community can meet each applicant's needs before admission, and the evaluation includes a National Sex Offender Registry inquiry or fingerprint records check. For a registered sex offender or violent offender, the community documents added safety measures such as monitoring, room and roommate selection and staff in-service. The community does not admit anyone whose needs exceed the care it is authorized or able to provide (63-.07), and does not admit above its licensed capacity or beyond the services shown in its DCH permit application (63-.05). Memory care admissions are made only after the memory care certificate is current. A physician examination is obtained on forms made available by DCH.

definitions.definition: The requirements an applicant must meet to be admitted, as set by 63-.15(1) and the community's licensed profile.
Care and treatment that requires a licensed nurse's or physician's ongoing attention, which the community is not permitted to provide as a community service.
A search of the national registry, or a fingerprint records check, to determine whether the applicant is a registered sex offender.

Documented steps the community takes to protect residents and staff when an admitted resident is a registered sex offender or violent offender, such as monitoring, room and roommate selection and staff in-service.
The maximum number of residents permitted by the community's DCH permit.

procedures: The first contact with a prospective resident or family is logged. Admissions staff give the community's licensed residential care profile, the services and rates list, and the list of conditions the community cannot serve (see ADM-04), before any application or deposit.

Admissions staff confirm that the applicant is 18 or older and screen at the outset for obvious exclusions (active TB, need for continuous nursing care, restraint or confinement needs, inability to participate in transfers or activities). If any exclusion is apparent, the administrator is told and the applicant is referred elsewhere with help to find alternatives.

The administrator confirms before each admission that the community has an open bed within its licensed capacity, and that for a memory care placement the community's memory care certificate is current and a bed is available in the memory care center.

The on-site manager or administrator meets the applicant and representative in person where possible, and visits or phones the applicant's current location to review the applicant's functioning, supports and care needs.

The administrator or on-site manager reviews the applicant's current medical information and obtains a physician examination of the applicant on the current DCH form. The completed form is received and reviewed before the resident moves in.

A nurse (RN or LPN) reviews the medical information, medications and orders with the administrator or on-site manager when there is any question about whether the applicant needs continuous nursing care or restraint, and documents the conclusion.

The administrator or on-site manager conducts a National Sex Offender Registry inquiry, or obtains a fingerprint records check, for every applicant before admission, prints or saves the result, and files it with the evaluation.

If the applicant is a registered sex offender or a violent offender, the administrator documents a written safety plan before any admission decision. The plan covers monitoring, room and roommate selection and staff in-service. The administrator decides whether the community can safely meet these needs and records the reasoning.

The evaluation form records the applicant's needs, how the community will meet them, and the staffing available, and records the administrator's or on-site manager's decision to admit or deny, with date and signature. The evaluation addresses the community's staffing plan, including whether staffing must be increased for residents who need assisted self-preservation.

The administrator denies admission if the community does not have the authority, staffing, physical plant or training to meet the applicant's needs, and explains the reason in writing to the applicant and representative with a list of other options. The denial is filed.

The community verifies that the applicant has no active TB through the physician examination and any screening required by the DCH form. An applicant with active TB is not admitted until a physician documents that the condition is resolved or non-infectious.
Admission is not conditioned on advance directive status, payment source (private or waiver where the community participates in the waiver program), or other factors unrelated to the criteria above.

Before move-in, the resident and representative receive and sign the admission agreement (see RR-04) and the Resident's Rights form, receive the grievance procedure and Ombudsman information, and are offered Georgia advance directive forms.

On admission day, the on-site manager opens the resident file and confirms all admission documents are in it, including the physician examination, evaluation, offender check, signed agreement, rights form and powers of attorney.
The admission assessment and care plan are started under ADM-02 and ADM-03, and any placement conditions, such as added safety measures, are communicated to staff who need to know.
The administrator reviews all admissions and denials quarterly for consistency with the criteria and reports the review to the QA committee.

responsibilities.duty: Decide on admission within permitted capacity and authority, approve safety plans and deny when needs cannot be met.
Conduct the evaluation, run the registry inquiry, collect documents and open the file.
Review clinical information and advise whether the applicant needs continuous nursing care or restraint.
Provide disclosures, screen for exclusions and log inquiries.
Examine the applicant and complete the DCH form.

documentation: Inquiry log and pre-admission screening form
Documented evaluation with admit or deny decision signed by the administrator or on-site manager
National Sex Offender Registry inquiry or fingerprint check result
Added-safety-measures plan for registered sex offenders or violent offenders
Physician examination on DCH form
Written denial and referral list, when applicable
Signed admission agreement and Resident's Rights form
Quarterly admission review in QA file

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: PCH (2–24 beds) and ALC (25+ beds): administrator, on-site manager, nursing staff, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To identify each resident's care needs and preferences at admission, to detect change early, and to reassess whenever needs change substantially, so the care plan and staffing match the resident's needs.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes an assessment of each resident's needs, covering family supports, ADL function, physical care needs, medical information, cognitive and behavioral impairments and personal preferences (63-.17). The assessment is the basis of the written care plan, which is completed within 14 days of admission and updated at least annually and whenever the resident's needs change substantially or the resident is assigned to a memory care center. Residents in a certified memory care center are reassessed on the triggers stated in the community's licensed residential care profile, which must call for reassessment earlier than the customary quarterly review (63-.19). Nurse hours on site are used for assessments, care planning, staff training and medication competency checks. Periodic or short-term medical and nursing services are not a community service; they are purchased by the resident from outside providers (63-.17). The assessment informs staffing: the community increases staffing as the number of residents who need assisted self-preservation rises.

definitions.definition: A written evaluation of the resident's family supports, ADL function, physical care needs, medical information, cognitive and behavioral impairments and preferences.

A change in a resident's physical, cognitive, behavioral or functional status that alters the care or supervision the resident needs, such as a fall with injury, hospitalization, new diagnosis, marked decline in ADLs, wandering or aggressive behavior.
A resident's ability to evacuate with staff help in an emergency; the number of such residents affects required staffing.
An event or condition listed in the memory care profile (and used for all residents) that requires a new assessment before the next scheduled review.
A part of the community certified by DCH to provide specialized dementia care.

procedures: The on-site manager, with a nurse (RN or LPN) where available, completes the needs assessment on the admission form during the pre-admission evaluation and updates it within 72 hours of move-in after observing the resident. The assessment is signed and dated.

The assessment covers each required area: family supports; ADL function (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, eating, mobility, continence); physical care needs; medical information (diagnoses, medications, diet, allergies, treatments); cognitive and behavioral impairments; and the resident's preferences for routine, activities, privacy, food and care.

Information is gathered from the resident, representative, physician examination, prior providers and direct observation. The resident and representative are invited to participate and their preferences are recorded in their own words where possible.

The assessment identifies the resident's ability for assisted self-preservation, including mobility and the need for staff help in an emergency. The administrator reviews this when setting the staffing plan and adds staff as the number of such residents rises.

The assessment results are used to complete the written care plan within 14 days of admission (see ADM-03). If the assessment shows the resident needs services the community cannot provide, the administrator follows ADM-04 and does not continue the admission without a safe plan.

A nurse reviews the medication list and diagnoses and flags any need that appears to require continuous nursing care, restraint or confinement for behavioral control, which are outside the admission and retention profile (63-.15).
Direct care staff watch each resident daily and record observations. They report any change in condition to the on-site manager or nurse on the same shift, using the change-in-condition form.

The on-site manager reviews every change report within 24 hours and decides whether it is a substantial change. If so, a nurse or the on-site manager completes a reassessment within 72 hours, or immediately in an emergency, and the care plan is updated.

Reassessment is always done after: a hospitalization or ER visit; a fall with injury or two or more falls in 30 days; a new diagnosis or medication change that affects function; a marked change in ADLs, continence, eating or weight; new or worsening confusion, wandering, aggression or exit-seeking; or an assignment to or from the memory care center.

For residents in the memory care center, the community follows the reassessment triggers stated in its licensed residential care profile, which call for reassessment sooner than the customary quarterly review. Staff are trained on these triggers and the profile is reviewed annually.

Every resident is reassessed at least annually, and the community also does a documented review of each resident's needs at least quarterly. Dates are scheduled on a tracking calendar maintained by the on-site manager.

Nurse hours on site are scheduled at the levels the rule requires: 8 hours a week for 1–30 residents, 16 for 31–60, 24 for 61–90 and 40 for more than 90. If a certified memory care center is operated, the center has its own nurse hours: 8 hours a week for 1–12 residents, 16 for 13–30, 24 for 31–40 and 40 for more than 40. The administrator uses these hours for assessments, care planning, training and medication competency checks, and keeps nurse time sheets.

Nurses do not provide periodic or short-term medical or nursing treatment to residents as a community service. If a resident needs such services, the on-site manager helps the resident or representative arrange them from an outside provider such as home health or hospice and records the arrangement.

The representative or legal surrogate is told of every substantial change and reassessment result the same day or as soon as possible, and the notice is recorded in the resident file. The resident and representative are invited to review the updated care plan.
