The administrator reviews assessment timeliness monthly, using the tracking calendar, and reports overdue assessments and trend data (falls, hospitalizations, behaviors) to the QA committee.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure assessments are timely, set staffing to match resident needs and schedule required nurse hours.
Complete or oversee assessments, track due dates and notify representatives.
Participate in assessment of health needs, flag needs outside the admission profile and advise on care planning.
Observe, report changes the same shift and follow the care plan.
Share information and preferences and take part in care plan review.

documentation: Signed admission needs assessment and 72-hour update
Reassessment forms with the triggering event and date
Change-in-condition reports and notification record
Assessment and care plan tracking calendar
Nurse hours schedule and time sheets
Memory care profile reassessment triggers (if applicable)
Monthly QA report on assessment timeliness

policies.title: Written Service / Care Plan
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (Ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (Ch. 111-8-63); administrator, on-site manager, RN/LPN, direct care staff, and all residents including Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP / SOURCE) residents.
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident has an individual written care plan that reflects assessed needs and personal preferences. The plan is the guide staff use to deliver care, and it is kept current and filed in the resident file.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops an individual written care plan for each resident within 14 days of admission, using the pre-admission screening, the resident needs assessment and information gathered during the move-in adjustment period (Rule 111-8-63-.17(3)). Direct care staff use the care plan as the guide to the resident's care. The plan is reviewed and updated at least annually, whenever the resident's needs change substantially, and when the resident is assigned to a memory care center. Each plan is developed with the resident and, when appropriate, the representative, legal surrogate and family. For waiver residents, the plan is also person-centered and is coordinated with the resident's waiver case manager or care coordinator. The signed, current plan is kept in the resident file (Rule 111-8-63-.24).

definitions.definition: The individual written plan describing the resident's care and social needs, how often services are provided, the resident's preferences, and who is primarily responsible for each service.
A device used to help a resident with mobility or function. Use requires an order from a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant, a written care plan entry and the resident's consent.
The first days after admission, when staff observe how the resident is adjusting and what help the resident actually needs. Observations are fed into the care plan.

A change in the resident's physical, cognitive, behavioral or functional status that alters the services the resident needs. Examples are a hospitalization, a fall with injury, new behaviors or a significant decline in activities of daily living.
A distinct unit or area of the community that holds a DCH memory care certificate and serves residents with dementia.

procedures: On the admission date, the administrator or on-site manager gives the RN/LPN (or the staff member designated to draft the plan) the pre-admission screening, physician report, resident needs assessment and any representative or waiver documents.

Within the first week, the RN/LPN or designated staff member meets with the resident and, when appropriate, the representative, legal surrogate or family to review needs and preferences. The meeting is documented.
The drafter records care and social needs, including the frequency of each service, for example bathing twice weekly with standby assistance or daily reminders for meals.
The drafter records the resident's stated preferences for schedule, routines, food, activities, privacy and how care is delivered.

Where the resident has specific behaviors, the plan lists them with the individualized, least restrictive interventions staff will use. Physical or chemical restraints are never listed as an intervention.

If the resident uses or needs an assistive device, the plan records the physician, NP or PA order and the resident's consent. A device is not used without all three: order, care plan entry and consent.

The plan names the staff position primarily responsible for each service. It records family or representative involvement in developing the plan, or notes that involvement was not appropriate or was declined by the resident.
The administrator or on-site manager reviews and signs the plan, and the resident or representative signs to show participation. All of this is completed no later than day 14 after admission.

For waiver residents, the administrator or on-site manager shares the plan with the waiver case manager or care coordinator. Any service or goal in the waiver person-centered plan is reflected in the facility care plan, and the resident's choices are documented.
A copy of the plan is placed in the resident file and a working copy is placed where direct care staff can read it. The resident or representative is offered a copy.
At each shift orientation and when new staff are assigned to a resident, the supervisor makes sure direct care staff have read the current plan. Staff initial or sign the plan review log.
The RN/LPN or on-site manager reviews each plan at least annually. The reviewer documents the update date and any changes on the plan itself so the evidence of update is visible.

When a substantial change occurs, staff report it to the on-site manager the same shift. The plan is reassessed and revised promptly, usually within 7 days. A revision is also made on assignment to a memory care center.
After any revision, the new plan is shared with the resident or representative and direct care staff, and the superseded version is marked and retained in the file.
The QA designee reviews a sample of plans each quarter for the 14-day deadline, required content, annual updates and consistency with the assessment. Findings go to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure each plan is completed within 14 days and updated as required. Sign each plan and keep it in the resident file.
Draft and review care plans, assess needs, order and record updates after changes, and advise the administrator when needs exceed what the community can serve.
Read and follow the care plan, report changes in condition or preferences, and record care delivered.
Participate in developing the plan and share preferences and changes in needs.
Audit plans quarterly and report to the QA committee.

documentation: Signed individual written care plan with the date of development, within 14 days of admission
Record of the plan meeting, including participants and any family involvement
Physician, NP or PA order and resident consent for each assistive device
Dated annual and change-of-condition updates, with prior versions retained
Staff plan review log
Coordination notes with the waiver case manager or care coordinator, where applicable
Quarterly care plan audit results

policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Community Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (Ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (Ch. 111-8-63); administrator, on-site manager, RN/LPN and all direct care staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] does not retain a resident whose needs exceed the care the community is authorized or able to provide, and to define how those conditions are identified, evaluated and handled.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not retain residents who need more care than the community is authorized or capable of providing (Rule 111-8-63-.07). Residents who need continuous medical or nursing care and treatment, or who need physical or chemical restraints, isolation or confinement for behavioral control, do not meet the admission profile (Rule 111-8-63-.15(1)) and may not be retained. The community provides assisted living, protective care and watchful oversight (Rule 111-8-63-.17(1)). Periodic or short-term medical and nursing services are not community services and must be purchased by the resident from outside providers (Rule 111-8-63-.17(11)). Outside home health or hospice staff do not count toward the community's required staffing ratios. When a resident's condition approaches or crosses these limits, the administrator or on-site manager documents the evaluation, notifies the representative, and begins referral or transfer under ADM-05 or ADM-06.

definitions.definition: Nursing care within the scope of a direct care staff person that can be completed within seven days or on an intermittent basis.
Ongoing medical or nursing care and treatment that is not intermittent and cannot be completed within seven days. A resident who needs it is outside the admission profile and may not be retained.
Care such as IV medications, central line management and complex wound care. It falls outside health maintenance activities and is not provided by community staff.
A drug used to control behavior or restrict movement that is not required to treat a medical condition.
Any device or practice that restricts a resident's free movement. Bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking of bedding and mitts count as physical restraints. An alarm wristband does not.
Harm to a resident. The term includes pressure ulcers that are not properly cared for.
The ability of a resident to get to safety in an emergency with staff assistance.

procedures: At admission, the administrator or on-site manager gives the resident and representative a written summary of the conditions the community cannot serve, drawn from this policy, and records that it was given.

Direct care staff report any change in a resident's physical, cognitive or behavioral condition to the on-site manager during the same shift. Changes include repeated falls, new wounds, weight loss, increased confusion, aggression, wandering, or new treatment needs.
The on-site manager notifies the RN/LPN, and the RN/LPN evaluates the resident within 2 business days of the report, or the same day for urgent changes.

The administrator or on-site manager screens each resident against the retention limits: continuous medical or nursing care; need for restraints, isolation or confinement for behavioral control; inability to take part in transfers; and care that cannot be completed within seven days or intermittently.

Staff do not use bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking, mitts or any other physical restraint, and do not give chemical restraints. If a physician or the family requests one, the administrator declines it and begins the evaluation steps in this policy.

Complex care such as IV medications, central lines or complex wound care is not provided by community staff. A resident who needs it must obtain it through an outside licensed provider, or the resident is evaluated for transfer.

Resident-purchased home health or hospice services may be arranged where the community can still meet the resident's other needs, the resident or representative consents, and the outside provider coordinates with the RN/LPN. The administrator confirms that the outside staff are not counted toward the community's staffing ratios.
The administrator or on-site manager checks that the community's staffing plan can still cover the resident's needs, including the effect of added assisted-self-preservation residents on ratios.

The administrator or on-site manager notifies the representative or legal surrogate the same day that a retention concern is identified. If the resident can still be safely served, the care plan is updated under ADM-03 with added interventions and a review date.

If the resident can no longer be safely served, the administrator or on-site manager makes the retention decision in writing, notifies the representative or legal surrogate, and starts referral to an appropriate provider with the resident and family.
Where the resident's safety is in immediate danger, the administrator follows ADM-06 for an immediate transfer. Otherwise the 30-day written notice process in ADM-05 is followed.

Wound care is monitored by the RN/LPN. Pressure ulcers that are developing or not healing despite proper care are reported to the physician and counted in the retention evaluation, since improper care of a pressure ulcer is an injury.
Staff never make a retention or discharge decision alone. The administrator, or the on-site manager in the administrator's absence, signs each decision.
The administrator reviews the census monthly against the retention limits and presents trends, such as repeated transfers for the same condition, to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Make and sign retention decisions, keep the staffing plan current, and make sure the community does not retain residents it cannot serve.
Collect change-of-condition reports, coordinate evaluations, and notify the representative.
Evaluate residents with changes in condition and advise on whether needs fall within limited nursing services.
Report changes in condition the same shift and never use restraints.
Take part in the decision and help arrange outside services or a new placement.

documentation: Written summary of conditions the community cannot serve, with the date given at admission
Change-of-condition reports
RN/LPN evaluation and the administrator's signed retention decision
Notice to the representative or legal surrogate, with date and method
Referral steps and outside provider coordination, including confirmation that outside staff are not counted in ratios
Updated care plan
Monthly census review

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (Ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (Ch. 111-8-63); administrator, on-site manager and business office; all residents including waiver residents.
policies.purpose: To make sure every discharge, transfer and relocation is carried out with proper notice, respect for the resident's rights, an orderly handoff of the resident's records, medications and property, and a refund under the admission agreement.
policies.policy: Each admission agreement contains a written discharge and transfer procedure (Rule 111-8-63-.29(1)). When a discharge or transfer is needed, the administrator or on-site manager contacts the resident's representative or legal surrogate. [AGENCY NAME] gives 30 days written notice of its intent to discharge or transfer a resident unless an immediate transfer is required, in which case ADM-06 applies. A resident who has no court commitment and no authorized representative may self-discharge by giving 30 days written notice (Rule 111-8-63-.25(u)). Refunds are made according to the refund policy in the admission agreement (Rule 111-8-63-.16). If an emergency forces relocation of the community, [AGENCY NAME] gives timely notice of the new address to residents, family contacts, representatives and DCH (Rule 111-8-63-.14). For waiver residents, the discharge process also respects the HCBS settings requirements.

definitions.definition: The end of a resident's stay in the community, whether initiated by the community, the resident or the representative.
Movement of a resident to another care setting, such as a hospital, nursing home or another residential community.
A transfer that must happen without the 30-day written notice because the resident's condition or safety requires it. See ADM-06.
A resident's own decision to leave the community. If the resident has no court commitment and no authorized representative, 30 days written notice is given.
The person with legal authority to act for the resident, such as an agent under a power of attorney or a guardian.
The movement of residents to another location because the building cannot be occupied safely. See the disaster plan.

procedures: The administrator confirms that each admission agreement includes the written discharge and transfer procedure before it is signed. The business office checks this during the admission file audit.

When the administrator or on-site manager concludes that a discharge or transfer is needed, for example under ADM-04, they contact the representative or legal surrogate by phone the same day and record the call.

The administrator prepares a written 30-day notice of intent to discharge or transfer. It states the reason, the proposed date, who to contact with questions, the resident's right to contact the long-term care ombudsman, and the refund process.

The notice is delivered in person or by certified mail, with a copy to the resident and the representative. The date and method are recorded. The 30 days begin the day the notice is delivered or received.

The on-site manager meets with the resident and family within 5 business days of the notice to talk about needs and possible placements. For waiver residents, the manager also contacts the waiver case manager or care coordinator, who is to help find a setting that meets HCBS standards.
Staff provide the resident and family with a list of suitable options and send requested records, with the written authorization of the resident or representative.
Direct care staff keep providing full care and follow the care plan throughout the notice period. The care plan is updated for the transition.

On the discharge date, the RN/LPN or on-site manager prepares the transfer packet: care plan, current medication list, last MAR, physician orders, advance directive and DNR orders, diet information, and contacts. Medications are released according to HLT-01.

The on-site manager and the resident or representative go through the personal property inventory and sign the release. Funds and valuables held in safekeeping are returned under RR-05 with a signed receipt.
The business office calculates any refund under the admission agreement and issues it by the date the agreement requires, with an itemized statement. See RR-04.

If a resident gives notice of self-discharge, the on-site manager accepts the written notice, confirms the resident has no court commitment or authorized representative, confirms where the resident is going, and offers help with referrals and records.

The administrator reviews each discharge for safety. Where staff believe the resident may be unsafe after leaving, the administrator contacts the representative and, when appropriate, the local Area Agency on Aging.

If an emergency forces the community to relocate, the administrator or designee notifies residents, family contacts, representatives and DCH of the new address as soon as it is known, following the disaster plan under GOV-01.

Within 7 days after discharge, the administrator completes the file: the discharge summary, notice copies, property and funds receipts, and the refund record. The file is retained under the community's record retention schedule.
The QA designee reviews all discharges and transfers quarterly for timely notice, documentation and reasons, and reports trends under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Decide on and sign discharge notices, ensure 30-day notice is given, and oversee emergency relocation notifications.
Contact the representative, coordinate placement help, prepare the transfer packet and complete the property inventory.
Prepare clinical records and medication information for the receiving provider.
Issue refunds under the admission agreement and keep the financial records.
Provide written notice for self-discharge and take part in planning.

documentation: Admission agreement discharge and transfer procedure
Record of the representative contact
Written 30-day notice, with date and method of delivery
Resident self-discharge notice
Placement referral list and records release authorization
Transfer packet checklist
Signed property inventory and funds receipts
Refund calculation and payment record
Emergency relocation notifications to residents, family and DCH
Discharge summary

policies.title: Immediate Transfers of Residents
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (Ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (Ch. 111-8-63); administrator, on-site manager, RN/LPN and all direct care staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a resident's condition or safety requires transfer without the usual notice period, staff act immediately, protect the resident's rights and wishes, notify the representative and document every step.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not keep a resident beyond the community's capability (Rule 111-8-63-.07). When a resident has an accident or a sudden adverse change in condition, staff act immediately, notify the representative or legal surrogate, and record the change and the response in the resident file (Rule 111-8-63-.26). Where the resident needs emergency care or can no longer be safely cared for, an immediate transfer is made without waiting for 30 days of written notice. This policy is applied together with the immediate-transfer provisions of Chapter 111-8-63. The community honors a resident's valid DNR order and advance directive, and follows the emergency sequence in this policy.

definitions.definition: A transfer to a hospital or other appropriate setting that takes place without the usual 30-day notice because the resident's safety or immediate care needs require it.
An accident or abrupt decline in a resident's physical or mental condition that requires immediate action.
A valid physician's do-not-resuscitate order that staff honor in good faith.
The person appointed in an advance directive for health care under O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq. to make health decisions for the resident.
A resident receiving services from a hospice provider.

procedures: Any staff member who finds a resident with an accident, injury or sudden adverse change stays with the resident, checks responsiveness and breathing, and calls for help from the on-duty staff. Staff start first aid within their training.
For an unresponsive resident who is a hospice enrollee, staff call the hospice first, then the health care agent, and then 911 and begin CPR unless a valid DNR order applies.
For an unresponsive resident with a valid DNR order, staff honor the order in good faith, do not begin CPR, notify the representative and the physician, and document.
For an unresponsive resident with a health care agent but no DNR, staff call the agent. If the agent cannot be reached, they call 911 and start CPR.

For an unresponsive resident with no hospice enrollment, DNR order or directive, staff call 911 and start CPR. CPR may be withheld only where death is clearly futile and no physician, authorized RN or PA is on site.

Staff keep emergency numbers and resident information where they are readily available, including the resident's face sheet, medication list, advance directive and DNR order. A staff member goes with the resident or sends the information so it is available during transport.

The staff member in charge immediately notifies the on-site manager and the administrator, who decide whether the resident can return or needs an immediate transfer. The RN/LPN, when on site or reachable, assists with the clinical assessment.

The administrator or on-site manager notifies the representative or legal surrogate immediately, not later than the time the resident leaves the building, and records the time, the person reached and what was said.
Staff send with the resident the face sheet, current medication list and last MAR, physician orders, advance directive and DNR order, and contact information for the representative and the community.

If the resident's condition suggests the community can no longer meet the resident's needs, the administrator makes that determination in writing, tells the representative and the receiving facility, and does not accept the resident back until the community can safely meet the resident's needs.
The administrator informs the waiver case manager or care coordinator for waiver residents, and the hospice for hospice residents, the same day.
Staff record the event, the response, who was notified and the transfer in the resident file the same shift, using the incident report form.

The administrator or on-site manager begins an immediate investigation into the cause of any accident, injury or death. The investigation summary is reported to the representative or legal surrogate. Copies go to the resident file and to the central quality-assurance file.

After the transfer, the on-site manager secures the resident's belongings and medications, inventories them with a second staff member, and follows ADM-05 and RR-05 for return of property, funds and refunds.
The QA committee reviews all immediate transfers and investigations each quarter for causes, response times and trends (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Respond immediately, call for help and 911 as the sequence requires, and honor valid DNR orders and directives.
Direct the response, notify the representative, send the transfer information and begin the investigation.
Decide on return or immediate transfer, ensure the investigation is completed, and keep the QA file.
Assess the resident, advise on the transfer and review the follow-up.
Make decisions for the resident as authorized and be available for notification.

documentation: Incident or change-of-condition report in the resident file
Record of the emergency response, calls made and times

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (Ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (Ch. 111-8-63); administrator, on-site manager, RN/LPN, certified medication aides, direct care staff and residents who self-administer.
policies.purpose: To make sure that all medications in the community are ordered, obtained, stored, recorded and disposed of safely and in line with Georgia rules.
policies.policy: A physician order with clear instructions is required for every medication, including over-the-counter products, before staff assist with or administer it (Rule 111-8-63-.20). Medications are kept under lock and key at all times, whether held by the resident or the community, except where a resident must keep a medication on their person for frequent or emergency use. Controlled substances are kept in a locked cabinet or box of substantial construction with a log updated daily. Medications are kept in original labeled containers, and unit or multi-unit dose packaging is used. New prescriptions are obtained within 48 hours of notice, and the MAR is updated within 48 hours. Unused medications are disposed of under current FDA or EPA guidance. Residents who can self-administer may keep and take their medications securely.

definitions.definition: Medication administration record, updated daily, showing each medication ordered and each dose given or refused.
A drug regulated under federal controlled substances law.
Medication prepackaged by the pharmacy in individual doses or in multi-dose form for the resident.
A resident's taking of his or her own medication while capable of doing so safely.
A pharmacist's quarterly review of each resident's medications, including removal of expired, discontinued or deteriorated drugs and those of former residents.

procedures: Before any medication is given or assisted, the RN/LPN or on-site manager confirms there is a written physician order with clear instructions, including for OTC products, vitamins and supplements.
When a new prescription is ordered, the on-site manager obtains it within 48 hours of notice, or sooner if the prescriber says so. The medication is checked against the order on arrival.
The MAR is updated within 48 hours of any new order or change. A second staff member or the RN/LPN checks the entry against the order and initials it.
Refills are requested at least 7 days before the supply runs out so doses are not interrupted. Staff record the refill request.
All medications are stored in a locked cabinet, cart or room. The key is held only by the certified medication aide or staff person in charge of the shift.
Duplicate keys are kept on site in a secure location known to the administrator and on-site manager. A record of who holds each key is maintained.

Controlled substances are stored in a locked cabinet or box of substantial construction, separate from other medications. A log is updated daily with each dose given. The count is checked at each change of shift by two staff members, and any discrepancy is reported to the administrator immediately.

Medications are kept in their original labeled containers and are not transferred or relabeled by staff. Unit or multi-unit dose packaging is used. Staff do not mix medications from different residents.

Residents who self-administer keep medications in a locked box, drawer or room in their living space. The RN/LPN assesses the resident's ability to self-administer and records it in the care plan. A resident who must carry a medication on their person for frequent or emergency use may do so with a physician's order.
Medication reference information, including descriptions, dosing, side effects and contraindications, is kept where medication staff can find it quickly.
Hospice liquid morphine on site is limited to 50 ml per hospice patient and requires a physician order. It is stored and logged as a controlled substance.

Staff dispose of unused, discontinued or expired medications under current FDA or EPA guidance. Controlled substance disposal follows applicable federal rules. Two staff members witness each disposal and sign the disposal record with the drug name, strength, quantity and resident name.
The consultant pharmacist removes expired, discontinued or deteriorated drugs and those of former residents during the quarterly review. The administrator keeps the pharmacist's report.
Sharps, such as lancets and insulin needles, are placed in puncture-resistant sharps containers and disposed of as regulated medical waste under the community's exposure control practices.
When a resident leaves, medications are inventoried by two staff members and released to the resident or representative only as the physician's order and law allow. A signed receipt is kept.
The administrator audits medication storage, the controlled substance log and the MAR monthly, and reports findings to the QA committee.

policies.title: Medication Administration and Staff Authorization (Certified Medication Aides)
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (Ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (Ch. 111-8-63); administrator, on-site manager, RN/LPN, certified medication aides (CMAs) and other direct care staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure that only qualified, verified staff administer medications, that their competency is checked, and that unlicensed staff who assist residents stay within the tasks Georgia permits.
policies.policy: Residents who can self-administer may keep and take their medications securely (Rule 111-8-63-.20). Staff assistance with self-administration is limited to the tasks the rule lists, and only for unit or multi-dose packaged medications. Only certified medication aides (CMAs) may administer medications on behalf of [AGENCY NAME]. Before a CMA administers medications, the community verifies the aide on the Georgia Certified Medication Aide Registry. Competency is checked at hire, quarterly and annually, and a pharmacist reviews each resident's drug regimen quarterly. Non-CMA staff who assist with self-administration complete documented medication training and competency checklists.

definitions.definition: An unlicensed staff member who holds Georgia CMA certification and may administer medications in the community within authorized tasks.
The state registry used to verify that an aide is in good standing and has no termination for cause related to medication tasks.
Limited help given to a resident who is able to take his or her own medication, as listed in the rule.
A skills checklist or observation by a qualified person to confirm that staff can perform medication tasks correctly.
A signed written plan, such as for EpiPen use, that tells staff what to do and includes calling 911.

procedures: Before any CMA is scheduled to administer medications, the administrator or on-site manager checks the Georgia Certified Medication Aide Registry. The aide must be in good standing with no termination for cause related to medication tasks. A printed or screenshot record is kept in the personnel file.
The administrator verifies the registry again for each CMA at least annually and whenever there is a concern about the aide's practice. Records are dated and initialed.
For a CMA who has been certified for more than 1 year, the RN, pharmacist or physician completes a skills competency checklist at hire. The result is placed in the personnel file.
A Georgia-licensed RN or pharmacist conducts random observations of each CMA administering medications at least quarterly, and documents them on a checklist.
A Georgia-licensed RN, pharmacist or physician completes an annual comprehensive skills review for each CMA. A CMA who does not pass is removed from medication duty until retrained and rechecked.
A pharmacist completes a quarterly drug regimen review for each resident. The administrator gives the findings to the physician and RN/LPN, and follow-up is recorded.

CMAs administer only the tasks authorized: oral, tube, ophthalmic, topical, otic, nasal, vaginal and rectal medications; insulin, epinephrine and B12 under physician direction and protocol; metered-dose inhalers; finger-stick glucose testing; a physician-ordered commercial enema; assistance with self-administration; and liquid morphine for hospice patients under a hospice physician's written order. All of this is limited to unit or multidose packaging.

A CMA does not administer any medication, route or procedure outside this list. If a resident needs a task outside the list, the CMA tells the on-site manager, who arranges for a licensed nurse or an outside provider.

Before every administration, the CMA checks the resident's identity, the order and MAR, the medication label and packaging, and the dose, route and time. The CMA records the dose on the MAR right after giving it, not before.

If a resident refuses a medication, or a dose is missed or given in error, the CMA tells the on-site manager and RN/LPN immediately, records it on the MAR, and the physician and representative are notified. An incident report is completed.

Staff who are not CMAs may assist only with self-administration and only the tasks the rule lists, for unit or multi-dose packaged medications. EpiPen assistance requires a written protocol, and staff call 911 after use.

Non-CMA staff who assist with self-administration complete documented medication training on the topics required by the rule. Competency checklists are completed at hire and annually, and records are kept in the personnel file.

The administrator keeps a current medication-staff roster showing each person's role (CMA or assist-only), registry check date, last competency check dates and last observation date. The roster is reviewed monthly.

A staff member who is not authorized, whose registry status is not clear or whose competency is overdue is not scheduled to give or assist with medications. The administrator adjusts the schedule so that a CMA is available on every shift where medication administration is needed.
The administrator reports medication errors, observation results and registry issues to the QA committee each quarter (see GOV-04).
